standard.title: Semicolons and dashes
standard.description: understand and use punctuation conventions including semicolons and dashes to extend ideas and support meaning
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can understand and use a range of punctuation conventions including colons and brackets (AC9E7LA09). They have not yet examined semicolons and dashes specifically — marks used to extend ideas within sentences and to create effects such as interruption, aside and pause in both formal and creative writing.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand and use semicolons and dashes to extend ideas and support meaning in their own writing.

nodes.label: Semicolons and dashes — function and effect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify semicolons and dashes in texts and explain the function each performs (linking closely related independent clauses; marking interruption, aside or pause).
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of a semicolon and one example of a dash in provided texts and explain what function each performs in that sentence.
nodes.typical_width: Understand and explain the conventions for using semicolons (to link related independent clauses without a conjunction) and dashes (to create interruptions, asides, pauses or emphasis) across a range of text types including formal prose and drama.
wider: Compare how semicolons are used differently in formal academic prose vs how dashes are used in informal or creative writing — and discuss why each punctuation mark is suited to its typical register
Investigate how creative writers deliberately use dashes in dialogue to create interruptions, hesitations and asides that reveal character or dramatic tension
Examine how the same content can be punctuated differently using semicolons, colons, brackets or dashes, and how each choice creates a different effect

response_modes.reason: Students often learn punctuation rules in isolation. Seeing semicolons and dashes in varied contexts — formal prose, drama, informal writing — helps students understand that punctuation choice is rhetorical (creates effect) not merely grammatical (follows rules).

success_criteria: Identifies a semicolon in a text and explains that it links two closely related independent clauses.
Identifies a dash in a text and explains the specific effect it creates (interruption, aside, pause or emphasis).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires purposeful use of semicolons and dashes in own writing. Students who cannot distinguish the function of each mark — or who conflate them — will deploy them randomly rather than purposefully at Node 2, producing errors that undermine the intended effect.

nodes.label: Using semicolons and dashes in own writing
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use semicolons and dashes accurately and purposefully in their own writing to extend ideas and create intended effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Write two sentences — one using a semicolon correctly and one using a dash correctly — and explain the effect each creates.
nodes.typical_width: Use semicolons and dashes purposefully in a piece of own writing (e.g. creative dialogue or a formal analytical paragraph), demonstrating awareness of the register and effect each mark creates.
wider: Create a piece of dramatic dialogue that uses dashes deliberately to show interruptions, asides and pauses, and annotate the effect of each dash choice
Revise a formal analytical paragraph by introducing a semicolon to improve sentence variety and flow, and explain the revision

Limited width — these punctuation marks do not vary meaningfully across further contexts at this year band. Extension goes deeper: examining how cumulative punctuation choices across a text create a consistent authorial voice.

response_modes.reason: Accurate punctuation use requires repeated practice across varied writing contexts. Understanding the rule and correctly applying it under pressure are different skills. Multiple writing tasks that require deliberate punctuation choices build reliable usage.

success_criteria: Uses a semicolon correctly to link two related independent clauses in own writing.
Uses a dash to create an intended effect (interruption, aside, pause or emphasis) in own writing.
